learningObjective: Trace why a hierarchical all-reduce combines values on fast local links before exchanging one partial result per group across the slower scale-out network.
mediumRationale: An original 360-unit-wide SVG keeps both fast groups, both numeric partials, the slower-network boundary, and all four final rank results simultaneously visible on a phone. A browser-reviewed Mermaid draft required panning and was rejected. Fixed, coordinated geometry makes the local-sum and final-distribution comparisons inspectable without interaction. No source artwork or measured performance is reused.

pages.insight: The slide motivates hardware scalability and mentions FSDP mixed-precision settings, but it does not show collective traffic, links, or topology.
The neighboring compute-optimization slide distinguishes fast on-chip SRAM from slower HBM, reinforcing hierarchical bandwidth as a concept but stopping at one accelerator.
The training-stack slide lists FSDP and ZeRO sharding alongside other systems techniques, but provides no network layout or reusable collective diagram.
The system-design modeling slide defines data and model parallelism at a high level, without mapping either axis to physical links.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page deck was text-searched and the candidate regions were inspected directly. Pages 106-108, 114-116, and 166-168 were reviewed as neighboring sequences. Pages 106 and 116 concern LLM data and re-scoring; page 114 concerns numeric precision; pages 166 and 168 concern data pipelines and serving. No slide provides an accelerator-network topology or hierarchical-collective figure, so no deck artwork is reused.

sources.title: NVIDIA Collective Communications Library: Overview and Collective Operations
sources.usage: Official documentation verifies that all-reduce reduces inputs across ranks and returns the result to every rank; the overview verifies support for topology-aware communication within and across nodes.
sources.license: Documentation was consulted for semantics only. No NVIDIA text, image, measurements, or figure layout is copied, and public availability is not treated as reuse permission.

sources.title: How to Scale Your Model
sources.usage: The Google DeepMind scaling text verifies the communication-bound scaling model and the need to choose parallelism for the hardware topology.
sources.license: The repository requests citation and a contributor agreement but does not provide clear figure-reuse permission. No text, data, or figure structure is reused; the shipped diagram is an original abstraction with attribution to the conceptual source.

sourceReview.notes: The visual is an original, vendor-neutral redraw synthesized from the article and cited semantics. It does not reproduce a source figure, benchmark, topology, or branded hardware design. Labels and arrow structure, rather than color, encode all three stages.

agentReview.reviewer: GitHub Copilot CLI (task 1.3 independent article review)
agentReview.summary: Selected one compact hierarchical all-reduce flow after independently reviewing the full article, deck, official NCCL documentation, and the Google DeepMind scaling text. The visual targets the article's hardest spatial inference: local aggregation reduces the number of participants that cross the slower network boundary.

implementation.accessibility: A labelled SVG title and description give all four rank identities, local sums 4 and 6, and final sum 10 on every rank. Numbered stages, a dashed slower-network boundary, literal values, and repeated rank identities preserve meaning without color. A 360-unit viewBox keeps the whole comparison together at 390 CSS pixels. Shared theme tokens and a direct caption preserve dark, static, and print semantics without implying a measured saving.
